'''Susan Margaret Gasser''' (born 29 March 1955) is a Swiss [[molecular biologist]] whose research concerns [[chromatin]] organization, [[epigenetics|epigenetic regulation]] and genome stability, with a focus on biomedical impact. She is Director of the [[Swiss Institute for Experimental Cancer Research|ISREC Foundation]] and a guest professor at the [[University of Lausanne]]. Her work examines how the arrangement and movement of chromosomes within the [[cell nucleus]] influence [[gene expression]] and [[DNA repair]].

Gasser directed the [[Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research]] in [[Basel]] from 2004 to 2019 and was professor of molecular biology at the [[University of Basel]] from 2005 to 2021. She has been elected to scientific academies including the [[French Academy of Sciences]], [[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]], and the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]].

== Early life and education ==

Gasser attended [[St. John's College (Annapolis/Santa Fe)|St. John's College]] in [[Annapolis, Maryland]], from 1974 to 1976, followed by the [[University of Freiburg]] from 1976 to 1977.<ref>{{cite web |title=Susan Margaret Gasser-Wilson – Curriculum vitae |url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Gasser_Susan/CV |website=Academia Europaea |date=11 January 2017 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> She subsequently studied at the [[University of Chicago]], receiving a Bachelor of Arts with honors in 1979 and completing an honors thesis in [[biophysics]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Wilson SM, Makinen MW |title=An electron microscope study of the fiber-to-crystal transition of sickle cell hemoglobin |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=944–948 |year=1980 |doi=10.1073/pnas.77.2.944 |doi-access=free |pmid=6928690 |pmc=348399 }}</ref><ref name="FMIprofile">{{cite web |title=Susan M. Gasser |url=https://www.fmi.ch/research-groups/former/emeriti/emeriti.html?group=42 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="TokyoTechGasser">{{cite web |title=Susan Gasser |url=https://www.irfi.titech.ac.jp/wrhi-archive/en/people/susan-gasser/index.html |website=Tokyo Tech World Research Hub Initiative |publisher=Tokyo Institute of Technology |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

She completed a PhD in [[biochemistry]] at the [[University of Basel]] in 1982 under the supervision of [[Gottfried Schatz]].<ref name="TokyoTechGasser" /> Her doctoral research involved developing an ''in vitro'' assay system for investigating the import of mitochondrial proteins, demonstrating its energy dependence and identifying compartment-specific protein-processing pathways.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gasser |first1=Susan M. |last2=Daum |first2=Günther |last3=Schatz |first3=Gottfried |title=Import of proteins into mitochondria: Energy-dependent uptake of precursors by isolated mitochondria |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |date=10 November 1982 |volume=257 |issue=21 |pages=13034–13041 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)33618-4 |doi-access=free |pmid=6215405}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Daum |first1=Günther |last2=Gasser |first2=Susan M. |last3=Schatz |first3=Gottfried |title=Import of proteins into mitochondria: Energy-dependent, two-step processing of the intermembrane space enzyme cytochrome b2 by isolated yeast mitochondria |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |date=10 November 1982 |volume=257 |issue=21 |pages=13075–13080 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)33624-X |doi-access=free |pmid=6752147}}</ref>

After a postdoctoral appointment at the [[University of Basel]] in 1982, Gasser worked as a postdoctoral assistant with [[Ulrich K. Laemmli]] in the Department of Molecular Biology at the [[University of Geneva]] from 1983 to 1986.<ref name="PSUGasser">{{cite web |title=Marker Lectures in Genetic Engineering scheduled for April 22 and 23 |url=https://www.psu.edu/news/research/story/marker-lectures-genetic-engineering-scheduled-april-22-and-23 |publisher=Pennsylvania State University |date=15 April 2019 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> Her research there concerned chromosome structure and the organization of chromatin loops, including the role of [[topoisomerase II]] in metaphase chromosome structure and adenine- and thymine-rich sequences in long-range chromatin folding.<ref>{{cite web |title=Uli K. Laemmli |date=29 June 2022 |url=https://mocel.unige.ch/research-groups/former-groups/uli-k-laemmli |publisher=University of Geneva |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="TopoII">{{cite journal |last1=Gasser |first1=Susan M. |last2=Laroche |first2=Thierry |last3=Falquet |first3=Jacques |last4=Boy de la Tour |first4=Edith |last5=Laemmli |first5=Ulrich K. |title=Metaphase chromosome structure: Involvement of topoisomerase II |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |date=20 April 1986 |volume=188 |issue=4 |pages=613–629 |doi=10.1016/S0022-2836(86)80010-9 |pmid=3016287}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gasser |first1=Susan M. |last2=Laemmli |first2=Ulrich K. |title=Cohabitation of scaffold binding regions with upstream/enhancer elements of three developmentally regulated genes of D. melanogaster |journal=Cell |date=15 August 1986 |volume=46 |issue=4 |pages=521–530 |doi=10.1016/0092-8674(86)90877-9 |pmid=3015418 |bibcode=1986Cell...46..521G |url=https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/unige:150933 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gasser SM, Laemmli UK |title=A glimpse at chromosomal order |journal=Trends in Genetics |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=16–22 |year=1987 |doi=10.1016/0168-9525(87)90156-9 |url=https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/unige:149382 }}</ref>

== Career ==

In 1986, she established a research group at the [[Swiss Institute for Experimental Cancer Research]] (ISREC) in [[Epalinges]], near Lausanne.<ref name="PSUGasser" /> She remained at ISREC until 2001, studying chromatin organization through yeast genetics, microscopy and biochemical methods.<ref name="FMIprofile" /> She continued these studies as professor of molecular biology at the University of Geneva from 2001 to 2004.<ref name="UNILGasser">{{cite web |title=Susan Gasser |url=https://www.unil.ch/dmf/en/home/menuinst/research-units/gasser-susan.html |publisher=University of Lausanne |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250221035041/https://www.unil.ch/dmf/en/home/menuinst/research-units/gasser-susan.html |archive-date=21 February 2025 |url-status=dead |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

Gasser became Director of the Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research in 2004, serving until 2019.<ref>{{cite web |title=Interview with Susan Gasser, FMI Director Emeritus |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=481 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=7 December 2020 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Dirk Schübeler appointed as new FMI Director |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=450 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=15 April 2020 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> She continued to lead a research group at the institute until 2021 and held a parallel professorship in molecular biology at the University of Basel from 2005 to 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Former Group Leaders |url=https://www.fmi.ch/research-groups/former/ |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

In 2021, she became Director of the ISREC Foundation<ref>{{cite web |title=Susan Gasser elected director of the ISREC Foundation |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=489 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=28 January 2021 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> and a guest professor at the University of Lausanne.<ref name="UNILGasser" /> Her work at the foundation includes support for the Agora Cancer Research Center, which brings together cancer researchers and clinicians from universities and hospitals in Lausanne and Geneva.<ref>{{cite news |last=Dowell |first=William Thatcher |title=Innovative Cancer Research in Switzerland: AGORA Rising |url=https://www.global-geneva.com/climate/innovation/innovative-cancer-research-in-switzerland-agora-rising |work=Global Geneva |date=16 October 2019 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

She has also held visiting appointments at [[Osaka University]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Projects for promoting international joint research selected |url=https://www.osaka-u.ac.jp/en/news/topics/2013/10/20131011_01 |publisher=Osaka University |date=11 October 2013 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> and the [[Tokyo Institute of Technology]].<ref name="TokyoTechGasser" /> In 2026, she took up a 5-year specially appointed visiting professorship at [[Tohoku University]] in [[Sendai]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Welcoming Professor Susan GASSER to Graduate School of Agricultural Science, Tohoku University |url=https://www.agri.tohoku.ac.jp/en/news/20260714_01/ |publisher=Tohoku University Graduate School of Agricultural Science |date=14 July 2026 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==

Gasser's research investigates the relationship between the organization of [[chromatin]]—the [[DNA]] and associated proteins that make up [[chromosome]]s—and the regulation and maintenance of the [[genome]]. Her laboratory has used the [[budding yeast]] ''[[Saccharomyces cerevisiae]]'' and the [[nematode]] ''[[Caenorhabditis elegans]]'' as [[model organism]]s, combining [[genetics]], [[biochemistry]], [[genomics|genome-wide analyses]] and [[fluorescence microscopy]] of living cells.

During her postdoctoral work, Gasser studied the role of [[Type II topoisomerase|topoisomerase II]] in the structure of [[mitosis|mitotic]] chromosomes and characterized DNA regions associated with chromatin loops.<ref name="TopoII" /><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gasser SM, Laemmli UK |title=The organization of chromatin loops: characterization of a scaffold attachment site |journal=The EMBO Journal |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=511–518 |year=1986 |doi=10.1002/j.1460-2075.1986.tb04240.x |pmid=16453673 |pmc=1166792 }}</ref> At ISREC, she investigated the organization of [[DNA replication]] origins and developed assays for studying replication in isolated yeast [[cell nucleus|nuclei]] and nuclear extracts.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Pasero P, Braguglia D, Gasser SM |title=ORC-dependent and origin-specific initiation of DNA replication at defined foci in isolated yeast nuclei |journal=Genes & Development |volume=11 |issue=12 |pages=1504–1518 |year=1997 |doi=10.1101/gad.11.12.1504 |pmid=9203578 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Braguglia D, Heun P, Pasero P, Duncker BP, Gasser SM |title=Semi-conservative replication in yeast nuclear extracts requires Dna2 helicase and supercoiled template |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=281 |issue=4 |pages=631–649 |year=1998 |doi=10.1006/jmbi.1998.1973 |pmid=9710536}}</ref>

Her laboratory showed that [[telomere]]s cluster near the [[nuclear envelope]] and examined how this organization contributes to [[gene silencing]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gotta M, Laroche T, Formenton A, Maillet L, Scherthan H, Gasser SM |title=The clustering of telomeres and colocalization with Rap1, Sir3, and Sir4 proteins in wild-type ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' |journal=Journal of Cell Biology |volume=134 |issue=6 |pages=1349–1363 |year=1996 |doi=10.1083/jcb.134.6.1349 |pmid=8830766 |pmc=2121006}}</ref> These studies identified roles for the Sir3 and Sir4 proteins in telomere positioning and integrity.<ref name="PalladinoTelomeres">{{cite journal |vauthors=Palladino F, Laroche T, Gilson E, Axelrod A, Pillus L, Gasser SM |title=SIR3 and SIR4 proteins are required for the positioning and integrity of yeast telomeres |journal=Cell |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=543–555 |year=1993 |doi=10.1016/0092-8674(93)90388-7 |pmid=8221893}}</ref> In collaboration with [[Michael Grunstein]], she investigated interactions between these proteins and the tails of [[histone]]s [[Histone H3|H3]] and [[Histone H4|H4]], contributing to a molecular model of silent chromatin formation in yeast.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hecht A, Laroche T, Strahl-Bolsinger S, Gasser SM, Grunstein M |title=Histone H3 and H4 N-termini interact with SIR3 and SIR4 proteins: a molecular model for the formation of heterochromatin in yeast |journal=Cell |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=583–592 |year=1995 |doi=10.1016/0092-8674(95)90512-x |pmid=7867066}}</ref> Her group subsequently examined how the concentration of silencing proteins within nuclear compartments affects gene repression.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Maillet L, Boscheron C, Gotta M, Marcand S, Gilson E, Gasser SM |title=Evidence for silencing subcompartments within the yeast nucleus: a role for telomere proximity and Sir protein concentration in silencer-mediated repression |journal=Genes & Development |volume=10 |issue=14 |pages=1796–1811 |year=1996 |doi=10.1101/gad.10.14.1796 |pmid=8698239 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It also studied the relationship between association with [[nuclear pore]]s and the activation of inducible genes, showing that positioning at the nuclear periphery can have different effects on [[gene expression]] and telomere length maintenance.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Taddei A, Van Houwe G, Hediger F, Kalck V, Cubizolles F, Schober H, Gasser SM |title=Nuclear pore association confers optimal expression levels for an inducible yeast gene |journal=Nature |volume=441 |issue=7094 |pages=774–778 |year=2006 |doi=10.1038/nature04845 |pmid=16760983 |bibcode=2006Natur.441..774T }}</ref><ref name="PalladinoTelomeres" /><ref name="LarocheKu">{{cite journal |vauthors=Laroche T, Martin SG, Gotta M, Gorham HC, Pryde FE, Louis EJ, Gasser SM |title=Mutation of yeast Ku genes disrupts the subnuclear organization of telomeres |journal=Current Biology |volume=8 |issue=11 |pages=653–656 |year=1998 |doi=10.1016/S0960-9822(98)70252-0 |pmid=9635192 |bibcode=1998CBio....8..653L }}</ref><ref name="NagaiNuclearPore">{{cite journal |vauthors=Nagai S, Dubrana K, Tsai-Pflugfelder M, Davidson MB, Roberts TM, Brown GW, Varela E, Hediger F, Gasser SM, Krogan NJ |title=Functional targeting of DNA damage to a nuclear pore-associated SUMO-dependent ubiquitin ligase |journal=Science |volume=322 |issue=5901 |pages=597–602 |year=2008 |doi=10.1126/science.1162790 |pmid=18948542 |pmc=3518492 |bibcode=2008Sci...322..597N }}</ref>

Gasser's laboratory developed [[time-lapse microscopy|time-lapse fluorescence imaging]] methods to measure the movement of individual chromosomal regions in living yeast cells.<ref name="HeunChromosomeDynamics">{{cite journal |vauthors=Heun P, Laroche T, Shimada K, Furrer P, Gasser SM |title=Chromosome dynamics in the yeast interphase nucleus |journal=Science |volume=294 |issue=5549 |pages=2181–2186 |year=2001 |doi=10.1126/science.1065366 |pmid=11739961}}</ref> These studies showed that chromatin moves continuously within the nucleus and that its mobility varies with the [[cell cycle]] and its attachment to nuclear structures.<ref name="HeunChromosomeDynamics" /> Chromatin organization and movement change upon [[DNA damage (naturally occurring)|DNA damage]] in a checkpoint kinase-dependent manner<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Dion V, Kalck V, Horigome C, Towbin BD, Gasser SM |title=Increased mobility of double-strand breaks requires Mec1, Rad9 and the homologous recombination machinery |journal=Nature Cell Biology |volume=14 |issue=5 |pages=502–509 |year=2012 |doi=10.1038/ncb2465 |pmid=22484486}}</ref> and depend on the recruitment of the INO80 [[chromatin remodeling|chromatin-remodeling]] complex.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=van Attikum H, Fritsch O, Hohn B, Gasser SM |title=Recruitment of the INO80 complex by H2A phosphorylation links ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling with DNA double-strand break repair |journal=Cell |volume=119 |issue=6 |pages=777–788 |year=2004 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2004.11.033 |pmid=15607975}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Seeber A, Dion V, Gasser SM |title=Checkpoint kinases and the INO80 nucleosome remodeling complex enhance global chromatin mobility in response to DNA damage |journal=Genes & Development |volume=27 |issue=18 |pages=1999–2008 |year=2013 |doi=10.1101/gad.222992.113|pmc=3792476 }}</ref> They also were first to show the relocation of persistent [[DNA repair#Double-strand breaks|DNA double-strand breaks]] to nuclear pores,<ref name="NagaiNuclearPore" /> and that both pores and remodelers contribute to the recovery of collapsed [[replication fork]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Cobb JA, Bjergbaek L, Shimada K, Frei C, Gasser SM |title=DNA polymerase stabilization at stalled replication forks requires Mec1 and the RecQ helicase Sgs1 |journal=The EMBO Journal |volume=22 |issue=16 |pages=4325–4336 |year=2003 |doi=10.1093/emboj/cdg391 |pmid=12912929|pmc=175781 }}</ref><ref name="NagaiNuclearPore" /><ref name="SuRecombination">{{cite journal |vauthors=Su XA, Dion V, Gasser SM, Freudenreich CH |title=Regulation of recombination at yeast nuclear pores controls repair and triplet repeat stability |journal=Genes & Development |date=15 May 2015 |volume=29 |issue=10 |pages=1006–1017 |doi=10.1101/gad.256404.114 |pmid=25940904 |pmc=4441049}}</ref>

Later studies showed that DNA damage can trigger histone degradation, altering chromatin structure and increasing access for proteins involved in [[homologous recombination]].<ref name="FMIHistoneDegradation">{{cite web |title=Histone degradation accompanies the DNA repair response |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=322 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=10 January 2017 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="HauerHistoneDegradation">{{cite journal |vauthors=Hauer MH, Seeber A, Singh V, Thierry R, Sack R, Amitai A, Kryzhanovska M, Eglinger J, Holcman D, Owen-Hughes T, Gasser SM |title=Histone degradation in response to DNA damage enhances chromatin dynamics and recombination rates |journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=99–107 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/nsmb.3347 |pmid=28067915}}</ref> These investigations linked changes in chromatin packaging and mobility to the mechanisms through which cells [[DNA repair|repair damaged DNA]].<ref name="FMIHistoneDegradation" /><ref name="HauerHistoneDegradation" />

In ''C. elegans'', Gasser's laboratory investigated how [[heterochromatin]], a form of chromatin associated with gene repression, is positioned within the nucleus during development.<ref name="TowbinH3K9">{{cite journal |vauthors=Towbin BD, González-Aguilera C, Sack R, Gaidatzis D, Kalck V, Meister P, Askjaer P, Gasser SM |title=Step-wise methylation of histone H3K9 positions heterochromatin at the nuclear periphery |journal=Cell |volume=150 |issue=5 |pages=934–947 |year=2012 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2012.06.051|hdl=10261/129114 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Her group showed that methylation of lysine 9 on histone H3, known as H3K9 methylation, contributes to the localization of heterochromatin at the nuclear periphery.<ref name="TowbinH3K9" /> The laboratory identified CEC-4, a chromodomain protein that selectively binds methylated H3K9, as a heterochromatin anchor at the nuclear periphery, connecting chromatin anchoring with the maintenance of cell identity during [[cellular differentiation]].<ref name="FMICEC4">{{cite web |title=How packing away DNA stabilizes cell fate decisions |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=289 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=2 December 2015 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref name="GonzalezSandovalCEC4">{{cite journal |vauthors=Gonzalez-Sandoval A, Towbin BD, Kalck V, Cabianca DS, Gaidatzis D, Hauer MH, Geng L, Wang L, Yang T, Wang X, Zhao K, Gasser SM |title=Perinuclear anchoring of H3K9-methylated chromatin stabilizes induced cell fate in ''C. elegans'' embryos |journal=Cell |volume=163 |issue=6 |pages=1333–1347 |year=2015 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2015.10.066 |pmid=26607792}}</ref> Subsequent studies examined how modifications associated with active chromatin help separate [[transcription (biology)|transcribed]] regions of the genome from heterochromatin in differentiated cells.<ref>{{cite web |title=A role for gene activators in 3D nuclear organization |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=408 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=22 May 2019 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Cabianca DS, Muñoz-Jiménez C, Kalck V, Gaidatzis D, Padeken J, Seeber A, Askjaer P, Gasser SM |title=Active chromatin marks drive spatial sequestration of heterochromatin in ''C. elegans'' nuclei |journal=Nature |volume=569 |issue=7758 |pages=734–739 |year=2019 |doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1243-y |pmid=31118512}}</ref>

Her group illustrated how H3K9 methylation suppresses [[repeated sequence (DNA)|repetitive DNA]] transcription and protects against [[genome instability]] associated with [[R-loop|RNA–DNA hybrids]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Epigenetic repression suppresses genomic instability |url=https://phys.org/news/2016-10-epigenetic-repression-suppresses-genomic-instability.html |work=Phys.org |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=10 October 2016 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Zeller P, Padeken J, van Schendel R, Kalck V, Tijsterman M, Gasser SM |title=Histone H3K9 methylation is dispensable for ''Caenorhabditis elegans'' development but suppresses RNA:DNA hybrid-associated repeat instability |journal=Nature Genetics |volume=48 |issue=11 |pages=1385–1395 |year=2016 |doi=10.1038/ng.3672 |pmid=27668659}}</ref> Using a ''C. elegans'' model of [[Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy]], the laboratory examined how altered chromatin anchoring by nuclear lamins affects gene positioning and muscle function.<ref>{{cite web |title=The importance of gene position for muscle development and integrity |url=https://www.fmi.ch/news-events/articles/news.html?news=444 |publisher=Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research |date=16 March 2020 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Harr JC, Schmid CD, Muñoz-Jiménez C, Romero-Bueno R, Kalck V, Gonzalez-Sandoval A, Hauer MH, Padeken J, Askjaer P, Mattout A, Gasser SM |title=Loss of an H3K9me anchor rescues laminopathy-linked changes in nuclear organization and muscle function in an Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy model |journal=Genes & Development |volume=34 |issue=7–8 |pages=560–579 |year=2020 |doi=10.1101/gad.332213.119 |pmid=32139421|pmc=7111258 }}</ref>

== Professional service ==

Gasser served on the research council of the [[Swiss National Science Foundation]] from 1993 to 2002 and chaired the council of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] (EMBO) from 2002 to 2004.<ref name="GasserGenderEquity">{{cite journal |last=Gasser |first=Susan M. |title=Lessons in chromatin organization and gender equity in research: an interview with Susan Gasser |journal=Epigenomics |date=2022 |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=331–337 |doi=10.2217/epi-2022-0063 |pmid=35259924}}</ref><ref>{{cite report |title=EMBO Annual Report 2004 |url=https://www.embo.org/documents/news/facts_figures/EMBO_annual_report_2004.pdf |publisher=European Molecular Biology Organization |year=2004 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> She was a member of the President's Science and Technology Advisory Council of the European Commission from 2013 to 2015,<ref name="FMIprofile" /> and of the [[Swiss Science Council]] from 2016 to 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=Prof Susan Gasser leaves the Swiss Science Council after eight years |url=https://www.isrec.ch/en/prof-susan-gasser-leaves-the-swiss-science-council-after-eight-years/ |publisher=ISREC Foundation |date=8 January 2024 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> She was a member of the [[ETH Board]] from 2018 to 2026.<ref>{{cite web |title=Federal Council appoints new vice president and member of the ETH Board |url=https://ethrat.ch/en/federal-council-appoints-new-vice-president-and-member-of-the-eth-board/ |publisher=ETH Board |date=5 July 2017 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> From 2019 to 2026, she was Chairwoman of the Strategic Advisory Committee of the Helmholtz Health Institutes in Germany.<ref>{{cite web |title=Staff members |url=https://wp.unil.ch/emf/staff-members/ |publisher=University of Lausanne |access-date=19 September 2026}}</ref> She has also represented Switzerland on the councils of the European Molecular Biology Conference and the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Strengthening ties with the science community in Japan |url=https://www.embo.org/features/strengthening-ties-with-the-science-community-in-japan/ |publisher=European Molecular Biology Organization |date=1 February 2023 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=EMBL Council and Finance Committee members |url=https://www.embl.org/about/info/embl-council/embl-council-and-finance-committee-members/ |publisher=European Molecular Biology Laboratory |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>

Her scientific advisory work has included roles with the [[Francis Crick Institute]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Susan Gasser |url=https://www.crick.ac.uk/about-us/leadership-structure/board/scientific-advisory-board/susan-gasser |website=Scientific Advisory Board |publisher=Francis Crick Institute |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> the [[Biozentrum University of Basel|Biozentrum of the University of Basel]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Advisory Board |url=https://www.biozentrum.unibas.ch/about/organisation/advisory-board |publisher=Biozentrum, University of Basel |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> [[Vlaams Instituut voor Biotechnologie]] in Belgium<ref>{{cite web |title=Institutional Advisory Board |url=https://vib.be/en/institutional-advisory-board |publisher=VIB |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> and the International Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology in Warsaw,<ref>{{cite web |title=International Advisory Board |url=https://www.iimcb.gov.pl/en/about-us/international-advisory-board |publisher=International Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology in Warsaw |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> among others. Outside academia, she served on the Board of Directors of [[UCB (company)|UCB]] from 2021 to 2025,<ref>{{cite web |title=UCB announces changes on Board of Directors |url=https://www.ucb.com/newsroom/press-releases/article/ucb-announces-changes-on-board-of-directors |publisher=UCB |date=15 January 2021 |access-date=19 September 2026}}</ref> on the Board of Directors of the [[Genomics Institute of the Novartis Research Foundation]] from 2014 to 2018,<ref name="FMIprofile" /> and as a member of the Nestlé Nutrition Council from 2007 to 2017.<ref>{{cite web |title=Shaping the future of nutrition |url=https://www.nestle.com/sites/default/files/asset-library/documents/library/presentations/nutrition_symposium/shaping_the_future_nov2008_bauer.pdf |publisher=Nestlé |date=November 2008 |access-date=19 September 2026}}</ref>

Gasser chaired the Swiss National Science Foundation's gender equality commission and helped establish its PRIMA programme to support women in academic research.<ref name="GasserGenderEquity" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Susan Gasser receives honorary doctorate from the University of Fribourg |url=https://www.unibas.ch/en/News-Events/News/Uni-People/Susan-Gasser-receives-honorary-doctorate-from-the-University-of-Fribourg.html |publisher=University of Basel |date=16 November 2021 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref> She has participated in mentoring programmes for women scientists in Switzerland and Japan and was a founding member of Women in Science Japan in 2019.<ref>{{cite web |title=Celebrating women in science in Japan |url=https://www.mdc-berlin.de/news/news/celebrating-women-science-japan |publisher=Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine |date=25 July 2019 |access-date=9 September 2026}}</ref>
